R067-01.notes: B restates the closing sentence ('feel least effective... sometimes the ones that last') from the other side, and 'not always' keeps the hedge. C is directly negated in paragraph 5. A goes beyond the passage, since there is no comparison with real words. D is never claimed. Passage facts: Ebbinghaus in the 1880s, nonsense syllables, retention intervals from about 20 minutes to 31 days, steep loss in the first day that then slows, and spaced relearning beating massed relearning are all accurate. Saying spaced lists 'stayed with him far longer' simplifies his savings measure but stays accurate.

R067-02.notes: C paraphrases 'chosen so that no meaning or association could help him' almost word for word. Replication (B) was arguably one of Ebbinghaus's real-world motives, but the passage never says so, and the stem asks what the passage says. A and D are unsupported.

flags.note: Wording: the stem asks which 'result' would have misled a researcher, but the choices are conclusions ('That rereading ... produces better memory'). A clearer stem: 'would most likely have led a researcher who tested students only five minutes after studying to conclude that:'. There is still one clear key.

R067-03.notes: At five minutes the rereaders were slightly ahead, so a researcher testing only then would wrongly conclude that rereading is better. B is true, but it is the one-week finding, which that researcher would never see. C is Ebbinghaus's finding, not this experiment's. D reverses the confidence result. These details match Roediger and Karpicke (2006): free recall without feedback, rereaders ahead at 5 min (about 81% vs 75%), recall group ahead at 1 week (about 56% vs 42%). One small simplification in the passage: the higher predictions from rereaders come mainly from their Experiment 2 (repeated study vs repeated testing), not the single reread-or-recall design. Because the passage says only 'the students' predictions', this is acceptable.

R067-04.notes: Paragraph 3 shows rereaders more confident but worse in the long run, which is a gap between confidence and results. C is tempting because paragraph 3 begins with 'however', but there is no new experiment; it reports another finding from the same study. A is about the wrong paragraph. B is extreme.

R067-05.notes: The next sentence defines the term: 'processed easily, and that ease feels like mastery.' A and B are the everyday senses of 'fluency' and are the intended traps. D is the opposite of the point, because fluency is mistaken for accurate memory.

R067-06.notes: The example illustrates 'not ... every struggle is productive.' B reverses the example's point, though real research on pretesting is more mixed. C is extreme and contradicts the passage. D is unsupported.

R067-07.notes: B is a near-verbatim lift ('stayed with him far longer than lists he crammed'). A reverses it. C and D are unsupported, and D is extreme.

R067-08.notes: Paragraph 4: a student may conclude that the method is not working 'even as the struggle is strengthening the memory.' A is the misconception the passage describes. Paragraph 5 says not every struggle helps, but that refers to material never seen; this student is recalling notes already studied, so the caveat does not weaken D. B overstates. C misreads the five-minute result.

R067-09.notes: A matches 'may be a poor guide' in tone and wording. C is the strongest trap, because the author is critical of comfort, but 'never know' is too absolute and the author hedges ('may', 'sometimes'). D is factually false. B is the opposite of the passage.

R067-10.notes: The structure is Ebbinghaus (paragraph 1), the modern experiment (paragraphs 2-3), the illusion-of-fluency explanation (paragraph 4), and the 'None of this means...' qualification (paragraph 5). A, B and D each fail on a part: there is no rejected theory, no personal story or tips list, and no failed solution. Minor fact check: 'a century later' is loose, since the 2006 study came about 120 years after Ebbinghaus and research on testing as a study method began in the early 1900s. Read as 'about a century later' it stays acceptable, so it is not flagged.
